subject: Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions

messages.author: 20758fda448fdbda
messages.subject: Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
parts:
I've looked at a few previous examples, and I'm still not understanding why Stan is throwing an error. Hopfully, it is just obtuseness on my part.

I have a dataset which includes a matrix (dataframe) of 10 columns of 100 numbers (fake losses) each. The idea is that each column is a new year, and for each column, there are 100 rows representing 100 observations. I am trying to build a simple model to see if I can recover the underlying trend in fake data I have created. If that works, I can start playing with real data.

As I am not interested in using matrix algebra, my understanding of the documentation is that the most efficient way to code this data would be as an array of length 10 of column vectors, each of length 100. I could then loop through the columns and take advantage of vectorized calls. I know my data is in the form of a 100 x 10 matrix (calls to dim show that), but when I run Stan, I get the error: 

Error : mismatch in dimension declared and found in context; processing stage=data initialization; variable name=Losses; position=0; dims declared=(10,100); dims found=(100,10)

The code to build the raw data is:

set.seed(68951)
library(dplyr)
library(reshape2)
library(rstan)
trend <- .05
theta <- 1e6
alpha <- 5
ScaleTrendFactor <- (1 + trend) ^ seq_len(10)
IndLoss <- rgamma(1000, shape = 5, scale = theta * rep(ScaleTrendFactor, each = 100))
Years <- rep(seq_len(10), each = 100)
Obs <- rep(seq_len(100), 10)
LossData <- tbl_df(data.frame(Years, Obs, IndLoss))
names(LossData) <- c('Years', 'Obs', 'Losses')
DAT <- list(N = max(LossData$Years), Obs = max(LossData$Obs), Losses = acast(LossData, Obs ~ Years, value.var = 'Losses'))

Just to ensure:

> dim(DAT$Losses)
 [1] 100 10

The stan code (stored in a file called "Gamma_Bayes.stan")  is:


data {
  int<lower = 1> N;
  int<lower = 1> Obs;
  vector[Obs] Losses[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower = 0> shape;
  real<lower = 0> trend;
  real<lower = 0> rate;
}
transformed parameters{
  real scale;
  scale <- 1 / rate;
}
model{
  vector[Obs] L;
  rate ~ normal(0.1, .1);
  trend ~ uniform(0.0, 0.25);
  shape ~ uniform(0.0, 10.0);

  for (i in 1:N){
    Losses[i] ~ gamma(shape, rate / pow(1.0 + trend, i));
  }
}

The call to stan is:

A <- stan(file = 'Gamma_Bayes.stan', data = DAT, iter = 20000, chains = 5, par = c('shape', 'rate', 'scale', 'trend'))

When I switch the order of N (10) and Obs(100) in defining the "Losses" array, Stan runs, but returns rediculous responses with neff = 2 and Rhats in the 1e6 zone. The same issues hold if I define it as a matrix.

What am I missing (and feel free to trout me with the entire printed manual if appropriate 8-) ).

Thank you.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
parts:
vector[Obs] Losses[N];

would have shape (N x Obs), so you want to give it a (10 x 100)
matrix.

It may not be fitting for other reasons.

You can always use print() to make sure things get read in properly.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
parts:
What's going on with:

vector[Obs] Losses[N];


is that it produces an array of size N whose entries
are vectors of size Obs. So it's (N x Obs). Same shape
as this:

matrix[N,Obs] Losses;

There's a chapter in the manual that goes over differences
between arrays and vectors/row-vectors.

- Bob

In the 2.7 version manual on page 40, we are saying that:
row_vector[N] b[M];

matrix b[M,N];

vector[N] b[M];
is the same as:
matrix[M,N] b;

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
parts:
Raghu,

The short answer is no, they are not the same shape. More details below.

On Tue, Jul 28, 2015 at 10:18 AM, Raghu Naik <naik....@gmail.com> wrote:
I need to fix my understanding here as I am new to stan. 

In the 2.7 version manual on page 40, we are saying that:
row_vector[N] b[M];
is equivalent (though more efficient than) to:
matrix b[M,N];

matrix b[M,N] is not well formed. The square brackets always describe the thing directly to the left of it. The matrix type requires a size.

This is well formed: matrix[M,N] b;

Here, b is a matrix that is M rows and N columns. These are different types in the underlying Stan C++ implementation. If you wanted to operate over rows, the first, row_vector[N] b[M], will be more efficient than slicing rows out of matrix[M,N] b.

Now are we saying (as below) that:
vector[N] b[M];
is the same as:
matrix[M,N] b;

Both give the same shape. Is that correct?

This is incorrect.

vector[N] is an N-vector, or in matrix terms, N x 1. So vector[N] b[M] looks like a matrix[N,M], not matrix[M,N].

Hopefully that helps.


Daniel

Hi Raghu, 

In addition to what Daniel said, to relate your example to the example Bob and Avi are discussing above, in

vector[Obs] Losses[N]; 

N is the number of vectors (each of length Obs) in the array Losses. In your example 

vector[N] b[M]

M is the number of vectors (each of length N) in the array b. 

The easiest way to remember it (I think) is that the value you supply in brackets right after the word vector/row_vector is always the number of elements in the vector/row_vector. This is true if you're just declaring a single vector/row_vector or if they're part of an array. 

Jonah

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
parts:
> On Jul 28, 2015, at 11:52 AM, Raghu Naik <naik....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Daniel / Jonah:
>
> Thanks for the quick replies. Very helpful.
>
> It seems that in these declarations the vector[N] / row_vector[N] component is guiding the output matrix shape and we are not making any shape assumption of the b[M] array. For that reason
>
> row_vector[N] b[M];
>
> is matrix[M,N] and
>
> vector[N] b[M];
>
> is matrix[N,M].

I can see how you could conclude that, but it's not at all how Stan
actually works. Analogies from R will not work. We coded Stan directly
in C++ so you need to develop your intuitions there.

There's a whole chapter in the manual to help you get started.
Here are the data types in Stan and what they are in C++:

matrix[M,N] a; // Eigen:Matrix<T, Dynamic, Dynamic>

is a matrix, with data stored contiguously in column-major order in
the underlying C++ app. It's also what you need for any matrix op.

real a[M,N]; // std::vector<std::vector<T> >

is a 2D array, with data stored non-contiguously in row-major order.

And finally

row_vector[N] a[M]; // std::vector<Eigen::Matrix<T, Dynamic, 1> >

is a 1D array whose elements are rwo vectors.

> If that is the case we may be better off reading these statements as
> • a N dimensional row vector with M-dimensional columns as elements for the first declaration and
> • a N-dimensional column vector with M-dimensional rows as elements for the second declaration.

> Instead, for example, if I read the second declaration as a M dimensional array with N dimensional vectors as elements, I do not get a clue about the output structure ?

The I/O is all encapsulated w.r.t. R. When you go to the dump
format, we use R's dump ordering. For JSON in Python, it's done
differently.
> of this declaration. Is it a rbind or a cbind of the M vectors in b? That was my problem in the first place that got me looking up the group threads.

Stan's written in C++, not R, so there are no rbind or cbind things going on anywhere.

- Bob
